34_marg1630: Origen. God is quick to do good, slow to punish. For though he could punish the guilty without any warning of the judgment to come, he never does so; but even when he has condemned them, he foretells it, that those who had been condemned by their transgression may be set free by penance. The Ninivites were sinners condemned by God: “Yet three days, and Ninive shall be destroyed.” For God would not punish the condemned in silence, but, giving them room for penance, sent a Hebrew prophet to say: “Yet three days, and Ninive shall be destroyed,” that they might not perish (that is, because they had been condemned), but by doing penance might obtain mercy. The Sodomites also and the Gomorrhites were already doomed to divine destruction, as the word of God to Abraham shows; yet the angels did what was theirs to do, wishing to save those who had judged themselves unworthy of salvation, and saying to Lot: “Hast thou here any of thine, son in law, or sons, or daughters?” etc. Nor were they ignorant that those would not follow Lot, but they showed their own kindness and love, and equally that of him who had sent them. We find something like it in Jeremias. For the time of his prophecy is to be noted, when he began to prophesy and when he ended. Someone will say then: What is the time of the history to me? Because he began to prophesy in the days of Josias the son of Amon, king of Juda, up to the thirteenth year of his reign. Then he prophesied in the days of Joakim, the son of Josias king of Juda, to the completion of the eleventh year of Sedecias, the son of Josias king of Juda, and his prophecy was extended through three kings to the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month. For God had condemned Jerusalem for its sins, and this was his final sentence, that it should be left to captivity. But since God is a lover of men and wills not that any should perish, before the time of the devastation was at hand he sent this prophet also to invite to penance. He sent the same man also under the second king after the first, and sent him also under the third. Captivity was now imminent, and still God was exhorting to salvation, granting room for penance even one day before; whence it is written: “Even to the captivity of Jerusalem, and to the fifth month,” Jeremias prophesied. Already the chains of the enemy had bound their hands, and nonetheless God said this: ‘Behold, you are made captives. Come, though late, do penance. Ask me, and I will spare you. I who delivered you up can rescue you from captivity.’ This also we can understand of ourselves. If we sin, we shall be captives. For to be delivered up to Satan as a sinner differs nothing from the Jews' being delivered to Nabuchodonosor. As God gave them over to the adversary because of their frequent impieties, so we are delivered for our sins to a spiritual Nabuchodonosor. Whence: “Whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.” Think how great an evil it is to sin, that you be delivered to Satan, who takes captive the souls of those who are forsaken by God, not without cause, that is, nor without judgment. For when he has sent rain upon the vineyard, and it has brought forth thorns instead of grapes, what will he do but command the clouds not to rain upon the vineyard? Our captivity also is therefore near, if we do not do penance, that we be delivered, that is, to Nabuchodonosor and the Babylonians; and while they are already close by, the words of the prophets, of the law, of the apostles, and of Christ himself exhort us to penance and call us to salvation. If we hear, we believe him who said: “And I will do penance for all the evil that I had spoken to do to them.”

34_marg1632: The other prophets, as Isaias, Osee, Joel, were before the captivity of the two tribes, that is, of Juda and Benjamin; others after, as Daniel, Aggeus and Zacharias. But Jeremias and Ezechiel prophesied when the captivity was imminent, the one in the land of Juda, the other in Babylon. Jeremias began to prophesy as a boy in the thirteenth year of Josias king of Juda, the son of Amon, and prophesied under him nineteen years, and under Joakim his son eleven years, and under Sedecias, who was the last of the kings of Juda, eleven years, to the fifth month in which Jerusalem was taken captive by the Babylonians. But the three months each of Joachaz and Jechonias (of whom the one was led into Egypt, the other with his mother into Babylon) are counted in the years mentioned above. And so from the beginning of his prophecy to the captivity of Jerusalem, in which he himself was taken, he prophesied sixty-one years, apart from that time in which he was led into Egypt and prophesied there in Taphnis, as is contained in this very volume.

34_marg1640: Say not, etc. Gregory. Some laudably seek the office of preaching, to which others are laudably compelled. For Isaias offered himself of his own accord, saying: “Behold, here am I, send me.” Jeremias humbly resists, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God,” etc. From each an outwardly different voice went forth, but not from a different fountain of love. For there are two precepts of charity: namely the love of God and of neighbour. Isaias, therefore, desiring to profit his neighbours through the active life, seeks the office of preaching. Jeremias, through the contemplative life, desiring to cling to the love of God, refuses to be sent to preach. The one, lest by speaking he should lose the gains of silent contemplation; the other, lest by keeping silent he should feel the losses of zealous work. But it must be noted that he who refused utterly did not persist, and he who wished to be sent saw himself first purged by the coal of the altar; lest anyone, unpurged, dare to approach the sacred mysteries, or lest one whom God has chosen proudly gainsay him under a show of humility. Since, therefore, it is difficult to know oneself purged, the office of preaching is more safely declined. Yet it ought not to be declined obstinately when the heavenly will is recognized to require its acceptance. Moses wonderfully fulfilled both, who both refused to be set over so great a multitude and obeyed. For perhaps he would have been proud if he had fearlessly taken up the leadership, or if he had refused to obey the one who commanded. On both sides, therefore, he was submissive; by measuring himself he refused to be set over the people, and yet by presuming on the strength of him who commanded he consented.

34_marg1641: And the Lord put forth his hand, etc. It must be noted that here the hand of God is put forth, which touches the prophet’s mouth, and it is said: “Behold, I have given my words in thy mouth.” But in Isaias it is written: “And one of the seraphims flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken with the tongs off the altar,” and he touched my mouth, etc. Because Isaias was of full age, and had unclean lips, and dwelt in the midst of a people that had unclean lips, one of the seraphims is sent, who touches his mouth not with the hand but with the tongs and the coal, and takes away his iniquities. But here the hand of God himself is sent, not to take away sins, which, because of his boyhood, he had not committed in great number, but to give the grace of speaking. Ezechiel, however, devours a book written within and without, that is, containing both the divine sacraments and the plain history. 34_marg1642: Two joyful things follow four sad ones; for good things could not be built unless the evil were destroyed, nor the best planted unless the worst were rooted out. For “every plant which my heavenly Father hath not planted shall be rooted up,” and the building that is not built upon a rock but upon sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. But that doctrine which the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and destroy with the brightness of his coming, namely every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine, he will destroy forever. And those things that are lifted up against the knowledge of God, and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will scatter and bring down, that in place of them humble things may be built, and in the place of the higher things that are destroyed and plucked up, things may be raised and planted that agree with the truth of the Church; of which: “You are God’s building, you are God’s husbandry.”

If you have understood the two peoples, namely Israel and the Gentiles, understand the transmigration of Israel in the people of the Jews, and of the same it was said: “I put her away and gave her a bill of divorce,” that is, that by leaving her he might establish an example. The law of Moses commands that a bill of divorce be given to a woman who displeases her husband, and that she be put away, and that then it be lawful for the husband to take another. So understand the Jews as receiving a bill of divorce, and therefore as being altogether forsaken by God. For where among them are the prophets, the signs of power, where the manifestation of God? No temple, no victims, no other worship of his expressed in the law. They were cast out of their lands, and so God gave them a bill of divorce.

If even now we judge our faith, and not the multitude and the will of men, and not the gathering, we shall see that in so great a number of churches faith is found with the greatest difficulty; for it is difficult for many to be good; whence: “many are called, but few chosen.” If therefore he says first: I put her away for the sins of Israel and left her in her defilement, but Juda, hearing what befell Israel, was unwilling to be converted to me; he speaks of our sins, who, reading what the people of the Jews suffered, neither fear nor say: if he spared not the natural branches, how much more will God not spare us? 34_marg1826: Gregory. The princes are those who depart from the Lord and are disobedient, who walk perversely and deceitfully. For of this melting it is read in Job: “Silver hath beginnings of its veins, and gold hath a place wherein it is melted.” In silver eloquence is signified; in gold, life or the brightness of wisdom. And because heretics so pride themselves on the polish of their speech that they are grounded on no authority of the sacred books, which are to us for speaking as veins of silver, because from them we draw the origin of speaking, he calls them back to the pages of sacred authority, that if they truly desire to speak, they may take from there what they are to say. And “gold hath a place wherein it is melted”: as if the true wisdom of the faithful, whose place is the universal Church, suffers tribulation from us who persecute it, but is purged from all the filth of sins by the fire of our persecution. Whence “gold and silver are tried in the fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.” Or, gold has a place wherein it is melted, because whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church can indeed suffer, but cannot become a martyr. Seek, therefore, O heretics, this place of melting; find this furnace in which gold is rightly purged. If you endure any bitterness or any tribulation for God outside it, you can be burned, but not purged. Whence: “The founder hath melted in vain, for their wickedness is not consumed,” etc.; and elsewhere: “If I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.” For some think wrongly of God, others dissent from the fellowship of their neighbors. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by schism. Whence at the beginning of the decalogue the fault of both is repressed, when it is said with the divine voice: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart,” etc., and immediately it is added: “Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.” For he who thinks wrongly of God does not love him. He who is at discord with the unity of the Church does not love his neighbor.

34_marg1900: Origen. The Lord, who maketh the earth by his power, etc. The prophet, taking in a certain manner three powers of God, power, wisdom, prudence, assigns to each its proper works: to power the earth, to wisdom the world, to prudence the heaven. In our earth, then (of which it was said, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return”), we have need of the power of God, without which it is impossible to carry out what is repugnant to the flesh. But when the members that are upon the earth have been mortified, then the spirit obeys the will. For by the spirit the deeds of the flesh are mortified. The Lord therefore maketh the earth by his power, which (as it is written in Job) he hath set upon nothing; whereby it is established that by the power of God the earth is held balanced in the middle of the world. I come also to the world, which in Greek is here called oikoumene, that is, the inhabited. I know a soul inhabited. I know one deserted. If then it has not God the Father and the Son saying: I and the Father will make our abode with him, and the Holy Spirit, it is truly deserted. But that soul is inhabited which is full of God and has Christ and the Holy Spirit. Hence David in the psalm of confession: “Strengthen me with a principal spirit.” “Renew a right spirit within my bowels.” “Take not thy holy spirit from me.” These things we have said in proof of this, that the inhabited, that is, the world, was built by the wisdom of God. For wisdom helpeth the just man, “having power over ten cities.” For “he that rejecteth wisdom and discipline is unhappy, and his hope is vain, and their labours without fruit, and their works unprofitable.” Let us labour, then, that our soul, being inhabited, may be raised up by the wisdom of God. For it fell from on high when we came into the place of miseries; it fell after we sinned. Finally, whoever or whatever is in this world fell before being raised up. For we all fell through sin into the world. But the Lord lifted up those who lay fallen, and by his prudence stretched out the heaven. Neither power nor wisdom is taken up in the stretching out of the heaven. Whence: The Lord by wisdom founded the earth, and prepared the heavens by prudence. There is therefore some prudence of God, which I would not have you seek outside Christ. For all things that are of God are Christ. He is his wisdom, he is power, justice, holiness. He is also prudence. But though it is one in the underlying reality, it is called by different names according to the variety of senses. For wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. For when it is called wisdom, it instructs you in the disciplines of things human and divine. When justice, he is signified as the distributor and judge of merits. So understand his prudence here, when it is teaching and demonstration of things good or bad or neither. And so now he is said to have stretched out the heaven by his prudence; whence: I stretched out my words, and you did not attend. For it asserts that there is a certain stretching out of words, as of the heaven. Whence: who stretcheth out the heaven like a skin. For our soul is stretched out, which before had been contracted. Those who bear the heavenly man are heavens. For if to the sinner it is said, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return,” why should it not be said to the just man: heaven thou art, and into heaven thou shalt return? Or if, on account of the earthy, it is said to him who bears the image of the earthy, earth thou art and into earth thou shalt return, why on account of the heavenly is it not said to him who bears the image of the heavenly: heaven thou art, and into heaven thou shalt return? Each of us has either heavenly or earthly things made for him. If they are earthly, they lead down to the earth, akin to them, the man who laid up treasure for himself on earth and not in heaven. But if heavenly, they bear their treasurer up to the region near to them.

34_marg1931: Origen. “A conspiracy is found among the men of Juda,” etc. If we have sinned, we who are called men of Juda because of Christ, it is said of us: A bond, or conspiracy, is found among the men of Juda and among the inhabitants. Jerome: since in the Church there are such persons in whom the snare of iniquity and the chains of sin are found, of whom it is said: “Everyone is bound with the chains of his own sins.” “They are returned to the former iniquities of their fathers.” He does not say simply of their fathers, but added “of their fathers, the former.” For we have two kinds of fathers, and there is one kind of the worst fathers. Before we believed, the devil was our father. Whence: “You are of your father the devil.” But when we have believed, we are made sons of God. If afterwards we sin, we return to the iniquities of the former fathers. “For everyone who commits sin is born of the devil.” So as often as we sin, we are born of the devil. Unhappy is he who is always begotten by the devil; but happy is he who is always born of God. For I will not say that the just man is born of God once only, but by each work of virtue he is always born of God. Our Saviour also is the brightness of glory. And brightness is not born once and then ceases; but as often as the light from which the brightness arises is kindled, so often the brightness of glory also arises. Our Saviour is the wisdom of God, and wisdom is the brightness of eternal light. So then our Saviour is always being born. Whence he says: “Before all the hills he begetteth me,” not, as some wrongly read, “he begot.” You also, in his likeness, if indeed you have the spirit of adoption, are always begotten of God, through each understanding, through each work, and are made a son of God in Christ Jesus.

Only let God the Spirit and God the Word come down and teach. “Make it known to me, O Lord, and I shall know,” as if: I cannot know unless thou reveal it. But with thee showing, I shall see the thoughts of each, and what they do, or what their will is. “Let us put wood on his bread,” etc. The bread of Jesus by which we are nourished is his word. Because, while he was teaching, some wished to place a stumbling block against his doctrine, crucifying him, they said: “Let us put wood on his bread,” etc. For when the crucifixion of the master is joined to his word and teaching, wood is put on the bread; and they indeed, plotting, say: Let us put wood on his bread. 34_marg1955: Consider the earth that is in thee, how it has been laid waste, and thou wilt see that after the coming of Christ the things have been fulfilled which were said: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.” Since now the earth does not work its works, nor are those things done among the just by which the flesh was formerly cherished, namely fornication, uncleanness, lust, etc. Whence: “I came not to send peace, but the sword.” Before he came there was no sword upon the earth, neither did the flesh lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. But when he came, and we were taught what belongs to the flesh or to the spirit, his teaching, like a sword sent in, divided the earth, that is, the flesh from the spirit, and laid it waste, because we bear about the mortification of Jesus in our body, and we do not live according to the flesh, but the spirit lives. 34_marg1960: Go and get, etc. A holy man is called the girdle of God, who was taken from the slime of the earth and is joined to his fellowship. And in a certain way he surrounds with greater diligence what seems unseemly in the Church, lest it lie open to the bites of the Gentiles and heretics. If this girdle touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, steeped in Assyrian moisture it loses its former strength and rots. And although it returns to the use of God, yet it will not be able to have its former fullness, not through the hardness of God but through its own fault, because it would not hear the word of the Lord. Let him therefore beware who can say: “But it is good for me to adhere to my God,” lest perhaps through negligence he be separated from his loins and cross the Euphrates and be given into the power of the king of the Assyrians, and be taken up not in the most solid rock but in a hole of the rock, corrupt and defiled, that is, in the filth and vices of heretics, and come to such rottenness that he can no longer return to the use and girdle of the Lord.

What is it then that Moses and Samuel are preferred to the other fathers in petitioning, except that these two alone in the whole course of the Old Testament are read to have prayed even for their enemies? The other is cast out of his rule and says: “Far be this sin from me, that I should cease to pray for you.” “If Moses,” he says, “and Samuel shall stand before me, my soul is not towards this people.” As if to say: I do not now hear even them on behalf of friends, whom I know by the merit of great virtue to pray even for enemies. Whence: “Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee; and whose shall those things be?” And nothing is more foolish than not to foresee the last things and to think brief things everlasting. 34_marg2107: Cursed be the man, etc. Those who think that souls were in the heavens and were cast down from a better state into a worse, use testimonies of this kind, namely, that it would have been better to dwell in the heavens than in earthly things and to be clothed with a body. But we, according to that of blessed Job, “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man child is conceived,” and “cursed be the man that brought the tidings to my father, saying: A man child is born to thee.” We expound this testimony thus: that it is better not to be than to be in torments. Whence “death is rest to a man whose way is hid,” for whom God hath shut his way, and “why is light given to him that is in misery?” etc., and it was better for him if he had not been born; not that one who has not been born is anything, but that it is better not to be than to be ill. For it is one thing not to be at all, another to be tormented without any intermission, just as we prefer quiet death to a miserable life. Whence Amos calls it a day of darkness, a day of affliction; and Jacob, because he lived in labor and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil. And Paul: “that he might deliver us from this present wicked world,” and “redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”
34_marg2108: Cursed be the man, etc. In the person of the prophet the changeableness of the wavering human race is signified; by his father, this world from which we are born is expressed. The man who announces our birth to our father is the ancient enemy, who, when he sees us wavering in our thoughts, incites the minds of the wicked to persuade our deception. And when he has seen us do weak things, he lifts them up with favors as if they were strong, and speaks of us as born males when he rejoices that we have become corrupters of truth or innocence through falsehood. Therefore he announces to the father that a male is born when he shows to this world the one he has persuaded to be made a corrupter of innocence. For when it is said to any sinner and proud man, “You have acted like a man,” what else is announced in the world but a male born?

34_marg2109: When he sent to him, etc. It is to be noted that in the prophets, and especially in Ezechiel and Jeremias, the order neither of events nor of times is kept; but out of order, what according to history was done later is related first, and conversely. Whence in the present place Sedecias, who was taken with the city of Jerusalem, is written as sending to Jeremias, at the time when Jerusalem was besieged; and afterwards the history is told of his brother Joakim, who reigned before him, and of Joakim, that is, of Jechonias, who was the son of Joakim, of whom it is said in what follows.

34_marg2129: Weep not, etc. Jerome. This seems to me to be said properly of Sedecias, of whom is the prophecy both of the present chapter and of the past one; under him the kingdom truly came to an end, under him the city was taken, and he himself was led to Babylon and died. This is Sellum, that is, consummation and completion, the son of Josias, king of Juda, who reigned after Josias his father. But Jechonias was not the son but the grandson of Josias, the son of Joachim; so that from the beginning of this vision, when Sedecias sent to Jeremias Phassur the son of Melchias and Sophonias the son of Maasias the priest, up to this chapter, we understand everything of Sedecias. 34_marg2130: Josias, a just king, had three sons: Joachaz, Joachim, and Sedecias. Since, then, three were taken captive, the Hebrews think this fits all of them, and they call all the sons of Josias Sellem or Sellum, that is, consummation or completion, because in them the kingdom of Juda came to an end.

34_marg2139: For if he were, etc. Jerome. Wretched Grunnius translated into Latin a single book of Sextus, a Pythagorean, a Gentile, and divided it into two volumes under the name of Sixtus the martyr. In it no mention is made of Christ, none of the Holy Spirit, none of God the Father, none of the patriarchs, prophets or apostles; and with his usual rashness and madness he named this book the Ring, which is read in many provinces, and especially by those who preach apathy and sinlessness. Since therefore the Lord threatens that he will cast Jechonias away from his hand like a ring, so I beseech the reader to cast away this wicked book. If he wishes to read it, let him read it as a philosopher, not as a churchman.

34_marg2142: Write this man, etc. Jerome. Christ was born of this man’s seed. Whence Gabriel: “The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father,” etc.; but not in his days, but much later. Of Joakim was born Jechonias, of whom Salathiel, of whom Zorobabel, and in order it comes down to Christ. But in the days of Joakim no son succeeded him as king, as he himself had succeeded his father; and until Christ none obtained royal power. For all were captives, and of the stock of David none reigned in Judea. Whence Josephus relates that the rulers were of the tribe of Levi, to whom Herod succeeded, the son of Antipater the proselyte; and afterwards, under Vespasian, the government of this race, or rather the semblance of a kingdom, was utterly destroyed.

They tear and scatter them by making schisms; they cast them out of the Church by unjustly separating them; they do not visit the sick; they withhold the hand from the penitent. God has mercy on them all, restoring the former pastures and taking away the evil shepherds.

34_marg2166: If therefore, etc. The Hebrew word massa Aquila translates “burden”; Symmachus and the Septuagint and Theodotion, “taking up.” Where therefore a thing is grievous and full of weight and labour, it is called a burden. But where prosperity is promised, or better things after a threat, it is called a vision or the word of the Lord; and it is plain from the very title of the prophecy, of burden or vision or word of the Lord, what kind of prediction follows. Since therefore the prophets were accustomed to announce sad things to sinners and so to provoke them to penance, but the Lord in mercy put off the sentence, the people, deceived by the fraud of the false prophets, thought that what the Lord threatened would not come, and turned a serious matter into a jest, and in mockery said to the prophets as they prophesied: Here again he sees the weight and burden of the Lord; and so it came about that it was no longer called a vision, but by way of jest a burden. The Lord therefore commanded that if the people or the prophet or the priest should ask Jeremias what is the burden of the Lord, he should say: You are the burden, and you the taking up. “For I will take you up and cast you away,” etc. “But if anyone shall dare to name the burden of the Lord, I will visit upon that man,” etc. Let every one therefore say to his neighbour: Not what is the burden of the Lord, but “What hath the Lord answered? and what hath the Lord spoken?” Because to each his own word and his own work will be reckoned as a weight. Whence: “By thy mouth thou shalt be justified, and by thy mouth thou shalt be condemned.”

Moreover, from words and from the interpretation of names things are often shown: as the names of Abraham, Sara, Peter, and the sons of Zebedee, being changed, signify a change of things; and in this prophet, phashur is called fear, or translation, or tenant, or stranger. But we, thinking with the apostle that the law is good and holy and the commandment good and holy, and that the God of both testaments is one, would rather refer it to those Jews who at the coming of the Lord believed or did not believe: so that those who cried out, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him,” are the basket of bad figs; but those who believed are referred to the good figs and the best basket.

In the eighth year of his reign he finally led Jechonias into captivity, with his mother and the princes; he reigned only three months after the killing of his father Joakim. Joakim was killed in the twelfth year of his reign.
34_marg2177: From the thirteenth year, etc. From the thirteenth year of the reign of Josias, who reigned in Jerusalem thirty-one years, Jeremias began to prophesy; under him he prophesied nineteen years. His son Joachaz succeeded him, who was at once taken by Pharao Nechao; Joakim his brother obtained the kingdom. In the fourth year of his reign this word of the Lord came to Jeremias. So then it was the twenty-eighth year of the prophet Jeremias since he began to speak to the people; and he never ceased, but every day, at earliest dawn and rising by night, he exhorted, and yet they did not hearken. But if, as the heretics will have it, the law was given once as a help, and precepts were established which by our own choice we either do or neglect, why does the prophet thrust himself in and daily repeat the commandments of God, if once received they suffice? But he shows that we always need the help of God, and that what was given once does not suffice unless it is constantly recalled by the admonition of the Lord.

34_marg2185: And when the seventy years are fulfilled, etc. Note that Jeremias prophesies not only against Babylon but against all the nations that were in Babylon’s army and fought against the people of God; whence in what follows, against Egypt, and the Philistines, and Moab, etc.
34_marg2186: Take the cup, etc. The cup of the fury of the Lord is propitiated by judgment: that all the nations that fought against the people of God drink of the cup of the fury of the Lord; whence Isaias: “Thou hast drunk of the cup of the Lord’s fury, and hast emptied it; therefore arise.” But this cup is drunk by all the nations so that they may vomit and rave; which a certain perverse interpreter takes in a good sense, after the manner of a purging draught, that it may force out whatever bile and phlegm and noxious humour is in the chest and restore the former health. He also takes Jeremias for a saviour, who gives the cup to all the nations to which he was sent, that, casting away idolatry, they might dedicate themselves to the worship of God; and what follows would show that this is contrary to holy Scripture. For the cup is not propitiated for a remedy, as that man raves, but for punishment.

34_marg2192: And the king of Sesac, etc. And the king of Sesac: as it were, all the nations round about will lie under the Babylonian empire and serve and drink of his cup. 34_marg2193: Babylon, which in Hebrew is Babel, is also called Sesac. For as we read the Greek alphabet in order to the last letter, that is, alpha, beta, etc., to omega, and again, for the memory of children, we reverse the order of reading and mix first and last, for example: alpha - omega, beta - psi, so among the Hebrews the first is aleph, the second beth, the third gimel, and so on to the twenty-second, that is the last letter, thau, before which is syn. We read therefore aleph - thau, beth - syn; and when we come to the middle, lamech meets caph; and, as we rightly read Babel, so, the order being changed, we read Sesac. But the vowel letters between beth and lamech, syn and caph, according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, are not put in this name; which perhaps the prophet prudently veiled, lest he stir up the madness of the Babylonians against himself, as the Apostle, writing of Antichrist against the Roman empire, says: “Only that he who now holdeth, do hold, until he be taken out of the way,” signifying the Roman empire, which according to Daniel is to be destroyed before Antichrist.

Because no inequality of wrath is found in God, he named the wrath of the Lord the wrath of the dove; for in order to show the force of the divine severity as undisturbed, he said also the wrath of a dove, as if to say: he who remains gentle exerts a strict judgment unshaken, and punishes while remaining meek; whence also at the last judgment, remaining unchangeable in himself, he is varied by no change or mutability. Yet he is by no means shown to the elect and the reprobate under the appearance of this same unchangeableness; for he will appear both calm to the just and angry to the unjust. For, their conscience bearing witness, they have failed within themselves; whence their minds look equally upon one and the same, but are not equally affected, because past justice shows him kindly to the former, and guilt shows him terrible to the latter.
34_marg2201: In the beginning of the reign, etc. This prophecy is earlier than the former, though under the same king. For that was made in the fourth year, this in the beginning of the same reign. Therefore in the prophets the order of history is not to be followed, since earlier things are said later and later things earlier.

34_marg2203: If so be they will hearken, etc. As if to say: perhaps they will hear and be converted. The word is doubtful and does not befit the divine majesty, but he speaks according to our feeling, and man’s free choice is preserved, lest by the foreknowledge of God we be compelled by necessity, as it were, to do something or not to do it. For it is not because God knows something to be future that it is future, but because it is future God knows it, as foreknowing things to come. And yet according to Jeremias, if God has foretold evils and the people have repented, or if he has promised prosperity and the people have neglected it, he would neither bring in the evils nor confer the prosperity. Like this is that: “perhaps they will reverence my son.”
34_marg2204: It is placed in our will either to do or not to do, so indeed that whatever good we wish, desire, and accomplish, we refer to the grace of God, who gives both to will and to accomplish. But if it suffices to walk once in the law given through Moses, as a foolish heresy supposes, how is it added, that the words of my servants the prophets be heard, who were sent after the law, and not once and by one secure, but always and by one careful?
34_marg2205: I will make this house, etc. As when the temple was built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and on mount Moria, that is, of vision, on which Abraham is told to have offered his son, the religion of Silo ceased, nor were sacrifices afterwards celebrated there; so when the Church was founded and spiritual victims were sacrificed, the ceremonies of the law ceased, and the city of the Jews was given for a curse, from which the Lord has freed us, redeeming us from the curse of the law, “being made a curse for us.”

34_marg2206: It is called new because those who sat in it and presided over judgment resisted the calumnies of the priests and false prophets.
34_marg2207: And the priests and the prophets spoke, etc. While the princes of the city were sitting in the gate of the temple, who had run together from the king’s palace to quell the sedition of the people, the assembly being gathered, the priests and false prophets accuse him, and if they had had the power of judgment they would have condemned the prophet also; whence we understand that those who seemed to be religious were more cruel, out of envy of holiness, than those who were attending to public necessities.
34_marg2208: Angry because he foretold that religion would perish, and the gains coming from religion. If at any time, on account of the commandments of God and the truth of the faith, priests or false prophets or a deceived people are angry with us, let us not greatly care, but let us carry out the sentence of God, thinking not of present evils but of future goods.
34_marg2209: And Jeremias said, etc. While they were accusing him and aiming at a charge of death, Jeremias speaks to the princes and to the people whom they had stirred up, prudently and humbly and constantly: he says he was sent by the Lord to speak against the temple and the city, and gives counsel that they do penance and the Lord change his sentence. He speaks humbly, saying: “Behold, I am in your hands,” etc. Constantly: “for in truth the Lord sent me to you.”
34_marg2210: Now therefore, etc. As if to say: if you are angry that I have spoken against the temple and the city, and you love the safety of the city and the temple, why do you heap sins upon sins, and make the city and its inhabitants guilty of my blood? If, then, at any time humility is needed by us from necessity, let us so take it up that we do not abandon truth and constancy. For it is one thing to insult a judge proudly, which is a sign of folly; another so to avoid an impending danger that nothing is taken away from the truth.
34_interl10261: as though the people had not been led astray by the priests and false prophets; but the people, having heard the reasoning, quickly changes its judgment, because the Lord promised pardon if they make their ways good; but the priests and false prophets persevere in accusation
34_marg2211: And the princes said, etc. The princes of the city and the people understand the truth of the judgment. But the elders, whose business it is to know true things, recount the history and compare Micheas to Jeremias, and show that he said graver things and suffered nothing from a just king; but all being converted to penance, the Lord changed his sentence. They also break the rage of the accusers, counting themselves among them: “We are doing a great evil against our souls.” As if to say: we shall not harm the accused, but our own souls, which we can free by a change of sentence.
34_marg2212: There was also a man. It is asked, since Urias prophesied the same things as Jeremias, and fled into Egypt, and was drawn back from there and killed, how could Jeremias, who boldly persisted in his sentence, escape the judgment of the crowd and of the princes and the counsel of the elders? To this it must be answered: the judgment of God cannot be known, when in the same cause one is punished and another set free. But perhaps Urias was killed for the condemnation of the accusers and of the people. Jeremias, however, was reserved for the judgment of God, that he might preach to the remaining peoples and provoke them to penance; as James was at once crowned with martyrdom, while Peter and the other apostles were reserved for preaching. And the constancy of the prophet is to be noted, because Urias, though drawn back from Egypt, does not change his sentence, and with death imminent nonetheless speaks what the Lord had commanded. But that he feared and fled is a judgment not of unbelief but of prudence, that we may not offer ourselves in vain to dangers; Christ also slipped from the hands of those who persecuted him, as the apostle says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
34_marg2213: And the king sent, etc. The question is asked how Joakim, a king of small dominion and of weakness, on the point of perishing, could send into Egypt and bring Urias out. But we ought to consider that Nechao, king of Egypt, had appointed him prince, and that this prophecy was made when he had begun to reign.
34_marg2214: So the hand of Ahicam, etc. Although Jeremias was delivered by the help of the Lord, it is nevertheless reckoned as a reward to him through whom he delivered his prophet; we believe this was in the reign of Joakim.
34_marg2215: In the beginning of the reign, etc. Many thought this was the beginning of the following chapter, but it is to be joined to the preceding one, so that whatever is reported as said or done at the beginning of Joakim’s reign, we believe, happened then.

34_marg2224: The allegorical interpreter, fleeing the truth of the history, interprets this place of the heavenly Jerusalem: that its inhabitants ought of their own will to take up bodies and go down into Babylon, that is, the confusion of the world, which is “seated in wickedness,” and serve the king of Babylon, that is, the devil. But if they will not, he would say, they will not bear heavy bodies, but will perish by the sword, famine and pestilence, and will not be men but demons. Let us follow the simple history, lest we be wrapped in certain deceptions.

34_marg2237: All the vessels, etc. Jeremias had said that the remaining vessels were also to be brought; here he affirms that what was carried away is to be brought back.
34_marg2238: Amen, etc. He wishes that to be done which the other lies about. This is what “amen” signifies, which the Lord often uses in the gospel; and he desires, for the prosperity of affairs, that the other rather than himself should speak the truth. Whence another prophet: “Would God I were not a man that hath the spirit, and that I rather spoke a lie.” But Jonas is saddened because he had lied, and is rebuked by the Lord that a lie was more useful than the ruin of so great a multitude. Yet lest he should seem to approve a false prophecy, he asserts the truth, without injury to the one who lies, by the example of others.
34_marg2239: Nevertheless hear this word, etc. He could have said: You lie, you deceive the people, you are a false prophet. But the other could have turned the same back upon Jeremias. So he does no injury; he speaks as to a prophet, as if to say: not only are we prophets, but there were many others before us, Isaias, Osee, Joel and Amos, who prophesied against many lands, announcing war and adversity and want; others also announced peace and prosperity, and these the outcome of events tested, not the flattery of a lie. The Lord also says through Moses that a prophet is shown by the end of his prophecy. And it must be noted that he rebukes the liar not with threats, not cruelly, but with confidence in the truth; and he puts it off to the future, that those who hear may await the outcome.

34_marg2240: And he took, etc. The prudence, humility and patience of Jeremias are to be considered. The false prophet does injury to the matter; he breaks the yoke from his neck, which he would not have done if it had been of iron. Jeremias is silent and hides his pain. For he had not yet received from the Lord what he should say; in which Holy Scripture tacitly hints that prophets do not speak merely by their own judgment but by the will of the Lord, especially of future things, the knowledge of which belongs to God alone.

34_marg2241: Supposedly. For many things in the holy Scriptures are said according to the opinion of the time in which the events are related, not according to the truth of the matter. Whence: “I and thy father sought thee sorrowing.”
34_marg2242: And the word of the Lord came, etc. When Jeremias had gone away and had swallowed down the injuries in silence, the word of the Lord came to him, not that he should speak with his own words to Hananias boasting in a lie, but that he should say, “Thus saith the Lord,” which the other had nevertheless said; but a lie always imitates the truth.

34_marg2246: This year, etc. If at any time we die, we are freed from the prisons of the body, according to that which heretics wrongly interpret: “Bring my soul out of prison,” because death is imposed as a punishment.
34_marg2247: Perhaps in the seventh month, which is wont to signify rest, they pretend he died, so that he is freed from the evils of the body, according to that: “Death is rest for a man.” But we know that the bodies of believers are temples of God, if the Holy Spirit dwells in them.
34_marg2248: And these are, etc. He intends to persuade them not to give heed to the false prophets who promised them a return to Jerusalem after a short time. But let them know that they will stay in Babylon for a long time.
34_marg2249: This little book of Jeremias is sent to Babylon to those who had been carried away with Jechonias, so that by the occasion of a royal embassy the prophet might complete his work and persuade the people of what the Lord had commanded him.
34_marg2250: To the remnant of the elders, etc. First the word of God is directed to the old men, then to the priests, third to the prophets, fourth to all the people; or the letter of the prophet is sent according to the order of their age.
34_marg2251: Mystically: after we have been cast out of Jerusalem, that is, out of the Church, for our sins, and delivered to Nabuchodonosor, of whom the apostle said, “to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,” etc., and elsewhere, “whom I have delivered up to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme,” we ought not to be wholly secure, or grow torpid in idleness, or utterly despair; but first to build houses, not upon sand but upon rock, such as the midwives built in Exodus because they feared the Lord; then to plant gardens, such as the Lord planted, paradise, and placed in it the tree of life, of which “she is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her,” etc. Third, to take wives, of whom one is wisdom, of whom Solomon says: “Love her, and she shall keep thee,” etc., and elsewhere: “Her I sought to take for my spouse,” etc. Nor is one wife enough; we ought to have several: let us add fortitude, temperance and justice, that we may beget more sons; and let us join our daughters, that is, good works, to husbands, that is, to the truth of faith; and begetting such sons and daughters, let us be multiplied, and destroying the things that are of a child, and growing into a perfect man, let us hear: “I write unto you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning,” and with the apostle let us say, “for in the gospel I have begotten you.” Let us therefore seek the peace of the Church, the city and our land, that we may deserve to return to it, from which we were carried away by the judgment of the Lord, that we might dwell in the confusion of error. For so we shall have peace. And the clemency of the Lord is to be considered: we ought to pray even for enemies, that we may do good to those who hate us.

34_marg2252: Take ye wives, etc. Jeremias, because the captivity of Jerusalem is near, is commanded not to take a wife, not to beget sons; whence the apostle: “The time is short. It remains that they who have wives be as if they had none.” But if, because of the shortness of the time, the use of wives is taken away from those who have them, how much more are those who have none commanded not to take them.
34_marg2253: Seek the peace, etc. Whence the Apostle: “I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men: for kings, and for all that are in high station: that we may lead a quiet and a peaceable life,” etc.
34_marg2254: Ezechiel testifies that there were false prophets and diviners and dreamers in Babylon among those who were carried away with Jechonias; yet when these letters were being sent, he was not yet prophesying, who began to prophesy in the fifth year of the captivity of Jechonias, which was the same as of the reign of Sedecias.
34_marg2255: Let not the prophets deceive you, etc. False prophets are those who expound the Scriptures apart from the sense of the Holy Spirit. Diviners are those who proclaim the conjecture of their own mind, and uncertain things of the future, as if true. Dreamers are those who do not hear that: “Give not sleep to thy eyes, neither let thy eyelids slumber”; their mind does not watch, weighed down by the slumber of error; to whom it is said: “Arise, thou that sleepest,” “and Christ shall enlighten thee.”
34_marg2256: Do not believe the false prophets who promise you a near return; for the seventy years will be fulfilled for you before you return.
34_marg2257: Seventy years, etc. We are involved in the confusion of the world for so long as it takes us to deserve to receive the rest of the sevenfold number; and when penance has been accepted, God fulfils what he promised and brings us back to our place, that is, to the Church; he who strikes that he may heal, who will give an end to labour and patience. For we shall call upon him and pray, and we shall be heard; we shall seek him with all our heart, and we shall find him. Some understand the seventy years according to that: “The days of our years in them are threescore and ten years.” When these have been fulfilled, we return to the Lord with our whole heart, and are heard; and then is the end of our labour and of our patience.

34_marg2262: To Achab the son, etc. The Hebrews say that these are the elders whom Daniel mentions, saying to one of them: “Thou that art grown old in evil days,” etc.; to the other: “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda, beauty hath deceived thee,” etc. “Who prophesy to you in my name” a lie, because, as they say, they boasted to the poor women that they were of the tribe of Juda and that Christ was to be born of their offspring; whence the women, enticed by desire, yielded, as if they were to be the future mothers of Christ. But this seems to stand in the way, that the king of Babylon is said to have fried them, whereas Daniel says they were stoned; whence by most, and almost all, of the Hebrews that is neglected as a fable; for they do not think that captives had power to stone their princes and prophets; and they affirm it to be truer what Jeremias says, that they were indeed convicted by Daniel, but the sentence was given by the king. But many of our own flock prophesy a lie in the name. They defile the wives of their fellow citizens, whom the old Nabuchodonosor fries in the fire of sin, according to that: “They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker.” But happy is he who bears the yoke of the Lord from his youth, who sits alone, who is full of bitterness, so that he may say: I sat not with the council of the malignant.
34_marg2263: In this chapter the allegorical interpreter dreams of the ruin of the heavenly Jerusalem, and suspects that the prophecy is directed to those who dwell in the Babylon of this world; because they did well, descending of their own will into these bodies, building houses, begetting sons, and being zealous for good works, after seventy years they will be sent into the heavenly Jerusalem. But he says that those who refused to descend to earthly things will suffer what the Lord threatens to Sedechias: because they refuse to imitate their brothers or to come into Babylon, the Lord will send upon them the sword, the famine and the pestilence, that is, the want of all things, and will make them like the worst figs, and will pursue them with an everlasting sword, and will give them over to vexation to all kingdoms; and they will not become men but demons, and will be a curse to all the angels who preside over the individual provinces; because in the heavenly Jerusalem they refused to hear the words of the prophets urging them to descend to earthly things, that, penance having been done, after the true sabbath they might possess their former place.

34_marg2264: To Semeias, etc. Semeias, from the place Nehelam, which is interpreted “torrent,” was led into Babylon with Jeconias, and prophesied a lie to the people, namely that they would soon return to Jerusalem. Therefore, since Jeremias had sent letters to those who were in Babylon, saying: “Build houses,” etc., and afterwards had added: “Let not your prophets deceive you,” etc., Semeias, understanding that this was written against himself, sends letters to Jerusalem, to Sophonias the son of Maasias and to the rest of the priests, asking why Jeremias is not rebuked by Sophonias, whose office it is to discern between false and true prophets; and it is ordered that he be shut up in prison and pay the penalty of a lie, because he has seduced the people. But Joiadas was the priest who handed the kingdom to Joas after the killing of Athalia, and killed the priests of Baal. As if to say: Why do you not imitate Joiadas? Why do you not kill Jeremias, the false prophet? For the Lord has appointed you in place of Joiadas, that you may discern by what spirit each one speaks. But the discernment of spirits is a spiritual grace.

34_marg2302: Statute. To set up a watchtower for oneself is to foreknow, by deep consideration, the coming struggles of the vices. And my elect one sets bitterness for himself when, even in the established peace of the virtues, seeing the evils that lie in ambush, he does not consent to rest secure. First, that he may not do any evil. Second, he considers lest he do good things carelessly; and after he has subdued the wicked things, he strives to subject even the right things to himself, lest, if it pass beyond the mind’s mastery, it be turned into the fault of pride. For from good things, through the fault of carelessness, evils are born: from learning, arrogance; from justice, cruelty; from piety, laxity; from zeal, anger; from meekness, sluggishness; and the like. “Direct,” he says, “thy heart into the right way.” The right way is the path of God’s commandments, in which one must walk, and not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

They conjecture this because the foundations of the city are to be laid from the tower of Anathoth, which is called Jeremias’s and is separated from Jerusalem by a distance of three thousand paces, as far as the torrent Cedron. 34_marg2320: Even to the gate of the corner, etc. At the corner the two walls of the city are joined; so it is said the city is built from the tower of Ananehel to the gate of the corner, because the Church, beginning from the height of grace, is built up to the entry and the regard of the Jewish and the Gentile people.
34_marg2321: Even to the gate of the corner, etc. Although the Church seems to have a lofty beginning, yet in this life the corners cannot possess the straight line of truth. For we stand in a corner while we live; and with the lines broken, it also goes out beyond the measuring line, over against the gate of the corner, upon the hill Gareb, which is interpreted sojourning or itch. In this we are signified as strangers and pilgrims, and as having itching ears and readily receiving the novelty of the worst doctrine. And it compasses Goatha, which the Septuagint interpreted as circuit, namely of the elect, the living stones, which are rolled over the face of the earth and are bound together by the corner stone; and you understand that it will go round the whole valley of Phagar, which is interpreted of ruins, and of ashes, so that although we seem to ourselves always to be on the hills, we may yet fear ruins and consider ashes, and say in penance: “I did eat ashes like bread.” And all Sedemoch, which Jerome turned into “the country of death,” dividing one name into two. For sade means country, and mooch means of death. But the country of death is the country of sinners, which goes on as far as the torrent Cedron, where the Lord was delivered up, which is interpreted darkness. See how many places the Church has, and that she will at last be “without spot or wrinkle” in the heavenly places. You hear of corners and itch, you hear of ruins and ashes, the country of death and darkness, and never glory. Finally it follows: even to the corner of the horse gate. For there is no true justice or sure victory in this world. The very corner of the gate, although eastern, whence the light comes forth, is called of the horses, to teach us that we need running and struggle, that at last we may deserve to hear with the Lord: “Thou hast mounted thy horses, and thy riding is salvation.” In the eastern gate and in the gate of the chariots is the holiness of the Lord, that we may then think ourselves perfect when we shall have said: “The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands; thousands of them that rejoice: the Lord is among them in Sina, in the holy place.” This building will remain for ever.

34_marg2380: Rabanus. Since in the preceding chapter the prophet had dealt with Sedechias and what was done under him, he now turns the narrative to the times of Joakim the son of Josias. Whence it is plain that he did not keep the order of time in the narrative, but according to the dispensation of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in him, he wished his prophecy to be written as the occasions required and as the matters fitted, as is done in many places, and most of all in the gospel, so that the reader may know that the sacred Scriptures were not composed by human arrangement, but by divine inspiration and ordering.
34_marg2381: Rabanus. To confound the pride of the Jews, who resisted the commandments of God, he sets before them the obedient Rechabites, who obeyed the precepts of Jonadab in all things, until by the necessity of the Babylonian army they were forced to enter Jerusalem; whence the Lord promises them that there shall not be wanting a man of the race of Jonadab standing in his sight all days. Mystically, however, the Rechabites signify those who by desire of perfection have gone beyond the commandments of the law. For the just, for whom the law is not made, are thus proved not to be under the law, but strive not only to fulfil the justices of the law but even to surpass them, so as to add voluntary things to what is owed. Hence Abraham would not accept what was rightly due to him of the victory, though he whose spoils he had brought back himself humbly offered it; hence David wept for his slain persecutors; hence Elias and Jeremias remained virgins; hence the sons of Jonadab are praised by the Lord for the obedience shown to their father, and good things to come are promised them, who, not content to offer tithes of their possessions, but rejecting the possessions themselves, offered their souls to God; for what exchange shall a man give for his soul? We ought therefore to know those from whom the legal commandment is not required, but to whom the gospel word sounds: “If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast,” etc. When we offer tithes, we are in a way held under the burden of the law, and do not reach the gospel height, which promises to those who obey not only the rewards of the present life but of the future. But the law promises the comforts of this life, saying: He that shall do these things shall live in them. The gospel, however, says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” It is not great if we abstain from unlawful things, but it is if we abstain from them out of reverence for him who, on account of our weakness, permitted them to us. For what could not be grasped by all was not to be commanded generally; for those who are great in the perfection of virtues can be crowned. But those who are little, and do not fill the measure of the age of the fulness of the body of Christ, although they seem to be hidden by the brightness of the greater, are nevertheless free from the darkness of the curses that are in the law, and are neither added to present evils nor punished with eternal punishment.
