When one speaks, we all in the Church hear one voice alike, but we do not all understand alike, but as the anointing of God teaches us of all things. The teacher or maker himself also does not speak for the instruction of man if he does not speak by the anointing of the Spirit. For it was said to Cain: “Thou hast sinned, be quiet”; but because, his faults preventing it, he was not anointed, he could hear the words of God but not keep them; so Joakim and his servants could hear the words of God with the ear of the body but not of the heart.
34_marg2386: And with his mouth he pronounced, etc. It signifies that the apostles and prophets suffered no need of thinking out or lack of speaking, but brought forth everything readily and easily; whence: “Take no thought how or what you shall speak.”
34_marg2387: And he cast it into the fire. Astounding is the wickedness of a hardened heart: those who ought to have been pricked to penance by the wholesome warnings delivered the words of the Lord to the fire, and heaped insults on the prophet who was teaching and correcting them, whom they ought to have honoured; because the wicked spirit, who is always adverse to the spirit of grace, hardened their hearts that they might not believe and do penance.
34_marg2388: But the Lord hid them, etc. Against him human presumption strives in vain. For “The Lord keepeth all them that love him; but all the wicked he will destroy.”
34_marg2389: Therefore thus saith the Lord, etc. A fitting vengeance, because he burnt the words of the Lord; so whoever resists the commandments of the Lord will suffer vengeance according to the hardness of his heart; for “what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap.” It is to be noted, however, that in Paralipomenon it is read that Nabuchodonosor led this Joakim bound to Babylon, and in the Book of Kings that Joakim slept with his fathers, and Joakim his son reigned in his stead. But Josephus seems to agree more with the words of Jeremias, asserting that Joakim himself, the father of Jechonias, was killed in Jerusalem by the king of Babylon, not led captive to Babylon. In the tenth book of the Antiquities he says thus: When the king of Babylon had entered the city he by no means kept faith, but killed the strongest and comeliest young men together with king Joakim, whom he also ordered to be cast unburied before the walls. But his son Joakim he made king of the whole province; and those who were established in dignities, to the number of three thousand, he led captive to Babylon, among whom was the prophet Ezechiel, still a boy. This then was the end of king Joakim, who lived thirty-six years. He reigned, however, eleven years. The successor of the kingdom, Joakim, reigned three months and ten days. But whether the aforesaid Joakim perished in Jerusalem or in Chaldea need not be inquired, since according to the prophet it is established that his dead body was cast out to the heat by day and to the frost by night, so that he who burnt the prophetic writing with fire should be scorched by the heat of the sun and the frost of the night.
34_marg2390: And Jeremias took another, etc. Rabanus. After the burning, that is, of the first; because, Judea being reprobated for its faithlessness, the books of the law and the prophets were preserved for the salvation of the Gentiles, to whom all the glory of the old testament has been transferred; because “all these things happened to them in figure: and they are written for our correction,” etc. And there were added many more words than had been before, because they have the history only, but we with the history have the mystical sense. For they have a veil over their heart when Moses is read, but we with open face behold the glory of God.
34_marg2391: And he reigned, etc. That Sedechias reigned eleven years after Joakim, who was surnamed Jechonias, not only Jeremias but also the Book of Kings and of Paralipomenon relate. For after Josias his father reigned Joachaz three months; after him Eliachim, who is also Joakim, his brother, eleven years; after him also Joakim’s son Joakim, three months and ten days; and after him Sedecias, his uncle, eleven years; but all were wicked and idolaters, and therefore they perished.
34_marg2392: Pray to the Lord, etc. That the Chaldeans lifted this siege when the Egyptians approached, Josephus makes plain, saying that Vaphres, king of Egypt, came to the help of the Jews: and so when the king of Babylon learned this, he moved his camp against him, and having afflicted the province and plundered its fortresses, he was coming with a great army to besiege the city of Jerusalem itself. But the Egyptian king, hearing that Sedechias his friend was besieged, having gathered the greatest strength of warriors, came to Judea as if to raise the siege; but the Babylonian, departing from Jerusalem, met the Egyptians, and having overcome them all in battle, put them to flight and forced them to leave Syria. And when the king of the Babylonians had departed from Jerusalem, false prophets deceived Sedechias, saying that the Babylonians would not fight against him again, but would return, namely those who were captives in Babylon, with the vessels of God which the king had carried off. Jeremias prophesied the contrary, and the truth.
34_marg2393: Wherefore, etc. Rabanus. They excuse Sedecias in vain, as though he sent Jeremias into prison not willingly but compelled by the violence of the people and the request of the princes, adducing in confirmation of this opinion that in the necessity of famine he ordered food to be given him out of pious affection; for he who was unfaithful and opposed to God could not keep faith with a man. For it is clear from his works that he did nothing pleasing to God, either in the fear of God or in love of neighbour, and therefore he justly suffered the vengeance for his sins.
34_interl10620: made a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven
34_marg2394: As those princes who put the prophet into the pit signify the demons, who always desire to plunge Christ’s faithful into the mire of vices and the filth of sins, so this Ethiopian eunuch, who, pricked by the fear and love of God, rescued the prophet, signifies the preachers from among the Gentiles, who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, and who, by the impulse of true charity, strive in word and deed and example to draw those unjustly oppressed out of the pit of perdition; which his name also bears witness to, for Abdemelech is interpreted “servant of the king”: of him, namely, of whom it is said, “a great King above all gods.” Whom the order of preachers serves by the word of the gospel, joining the Gentiles to the faith. But that, helped by divine admonitions and the examples of those before us, we are delivered from the depth of this life, is well figured through Jeremias, for when he is lifted out of the pit, ropes and old rags are let down to him. For by the ropes are figured the precepts of God, which, because they convict and rescue us when set in sins, as it were bind and draw, constrain and lift. But lest, bound with these ropes, he be also hurt while being drawn, old rags are also put with them, because, lest the divine precepts terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers comfort us, so that by comparison with them we may presume that we can do what we dread from our weakness. If therefore we hasten to be lifted out of this depth, let us be bound with ropes, that is, constrained by the Lord’s precepts. Let the old rags also be there, that the ropes may be better held, that is, let us be conformed to the examples of those before us, lest subtle precepts wound us in our weakness. Whence: “Remember your prelates who have spoken the word of God to you; whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.”
34_interl10624: that is, preachers from among the Gentiles
34_interl10625: that is, the examples of the ancient fathers
34_marg2395: If thou wilt take a resolution and go out, etc. The prophet, foreseeing that the city was to be handed over into the hands of the Chaldeans, advised the king to surrender himself into the hands of the king of Babylon, so that he might thus soften his furious mind and receive a lighter sentence; but the hardened mind could not be corrected.
34_marg2396: And king Sedecias said, etc. It is clear that Sedecias showed mercy to Jeremias without pure affection. For if he truly loved him, he would not hand him over to the princes. Fruitless therefore was his feigned mercy, like that of Pilate, who in the passion of the Lord washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this man.” But afterwards he handed him over to the Jews, scourged, to be crucified.
34_marg2397: It signifies that fleeting thought and voluptuous counsellors sink the steps of our works in the slipperiness of carnal desires and the mire of vices, and when they see us sunk they depart from us, because to the lost they can give no counsel, since they strove for this alone, to cast us headlong into the abyss of sin. If therefore we are unwilling, by the counsel of the divine Scriptures, to correct our sins and free our souls from perdition by penance, we shall be led out to the Chaldeans, which is interpreted “demons,” with our wives, that is, with carnal concupiscences, and our sons, that is, with depraved acts, and we shall be handed over bound into the hand of the king of eternal confusion, who will burn our city, that is, flesh and soul together, with unquenchable fire.
34_interl10637: of the devil of everlasting confusion
34_interl10638: that is, the soul together with the body
34_marg2398: Rabanus. To the proud and contemptuous God renders punishments, to the meek and humble consolations, which is clear in king Sedecias and in the prophet Jeremias and in the sentence of king Nabuchodonosor. Nor is it wonderful if through the same things he renders different things to different men, since through the same elements, chosen according to the quality of merits, he repays the elect and the reprobate differently: the water of the Red Sea preserved the Israelites unharmed, the same killed the Egyptians; the flame of the furnace burned the ministers of the king of Babylon, and preserved the children blessing God in the midst of the fire. Whence the wise man says in the praises of God: “For the creature serving thee the Creator, is made fierce against the unjust for their punishment; and abateth its strength for the benefit of them that trust in thee.”
34_marg2399: They that hope in the Lord shall not be confounded. Let all that do unjust things be confounded. Behold, the princes who sought the life of Jeremias are made captives; the eunuch who had delivered him obtained perfect liberty. So also, when the holy preachers are delivered, their persecutors will be punished with eternal vengeance.
34_marg2400: The word that was made, etc. It is asked how this word of the Lord is said to have been made to Jeremias the prophet. For it is not shown what this word was or what it made known; whence, unless I am mistaken, it is given to be understood that the prophet wished to signify secretly, by this word spoken to him, that his deliverance had been brought about through the captain of the soldiery by the divine will, as Nabuzardan himself says: “The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place,” etc. If therefore those who sinned against the Lord and did not obey were taken captive according to the word of the Lord, he who rebuked sinners and obeyed the Lord was set free according to the word of the Lord.
34_marg2401: The devastation of the city, the destruction, and the captivity of the people and of the faithless king having been described, there follows what was done concerning Jeremias, and concerning the remnant of the people, whom the prophet warned, by the word of the Lord, to stay in their own land and serve the king of Babylon. But they preferred to go into Egypt, where Nabuchodonosor afterwards slew them and laid Egypt itself waste.
34_marg2402: Rabanus. The mercies of the Lord are many, and his judgments are a great deep; as he justly rebuked the transgressors of the law, so he mercifully gave comfort to the humble and obedient. For through those very enemies by whom he punished the faithless king and his ministers, he appointed Godolias as protector of the remnant of the people. Mystically, moreover, Godolias, which is interpreted “magnified by the Lord,” signifies the preachers of the Lord, who are set in authority by the divine will, so that those who fear God may have refuge and comfort. These lay down their life for those under them, and set against the faithless the shield of protection, persisting faithfully in their office even to death, as Godolias, the innocent, was slain by the faithless Ismahel.
34_marg2403: And it came to pass, etc. Gregory. This deceit was done historically then by Ismahel, but is done spiritually every day by the devil. It must be known that the devil pursues our good deeds in three ways, so that what is rightly done before men may be spoiled in the sight of the eternal judge. Sometimes he defiles the intention, so that the action that follows is unclean from its origin. But if he does not prevail in this, he sets himself against it in the action itself, as on the way, so that when someone walks more securely by the purpose of his mind, a vice secretly joined to it destroys him as if from an ambush. Sometimes, however, he neither spoils the intention nor trips him on the way, but at the end of the action [he strikes] the good work; whence: “In this way wherein I walked, the proud have hidden a snare for me.” Which Jeremias well hints at, who, while he related what was done outside, showed what is done within, saying: “There came eighty men from Sichem,” etc. They shave the beard who withdraw from themselves confidence in their own strength. They rend their garments who do not spare themselves the tearing of inward beauty. They come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to present prayer with works in the sacrifice of God. But yet if they do not know how to look carefully to themselves on the way of holy devotion, Ismahel the son of Nathanias comes to meet them; because any malignant spirit, begotten by the examples of its former self, that is, Satan, in the error of pride, sets itself against them to deceive. Of whom it is said: “Weeping all along as he went,” because thou devourest minds [that he may prevail to destroy by striking], he hides himself under the veil of virtue, and while he pretends to agree with those who truly mourn, admitted more securely to the inmost parts of the heart, he kills what lies hidden within of virtue; because for the most part he promises to carry them on to higher things; whence: he is said to have said, “Come to Godolias the son of Ahicam”; and while he promises greater things, he takes away even the least; whence it is said: “When they were come to the midst of the city, he slew them.” Therefore he slew in the midst of the city the men coming to offer gifts to God; because intentions given to divine things, unless they guard themselves with great circumspection, while the enemy steals upon them, lose life on the very way, when they carry the offering of devotion. From his hand there is no escape unless one quickly returns to penance. Whence it is plainly added: “Ten men were found among them,” etc. For the treasure in the field is hope in penance, which, because it is not seen, is held as if dug into the earth of the heart. Those therefore who had treasures in the field were saved. For those who afterwards return to lamentation after the fault of their incaution do not die as captives. But when the ancient enemy neither strikes at the beginning of the intention nor kills on the way of the action, he stretches harder snares at the end, and besieges him the more wickedly the more he sees that this alone remains to him to deceive. These snares set at his end the prophet saw when he said: “They shall watch my heel”; for by the heel, which is the end of the body, the end of the action is signified.
34_interl10640: not having confidence in their own strength
34_interl10646: because he hides himself under a veil of virtue and pretends to agree with the mourning men
34_interl10647: because he promises to lead them to higher things, he who even takes away the least.
34_interl10648: in the very course of the action.
34_interl10650: whomever the devil deceitfully infects, he casts into the place of brimstone and eternal fire.
34_interl10652: namely the faithful, remaining in contemplation or meditation of the law, or on the watchtower of the virtues.
34_interl10655: which means “people of mourning”; for he makes captives companions of the perdition of the damned, who stand in eternal mourning.
34_interl10657: namely holy teachers, strengthened by the grace and mercy of God, who by fighting against spiritual wickednesses lead captives back to the Church.
34_interl10659: “Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.”
34_marg2404: This flight of the remnant, and their passage into Egypt against the word of the Lord, which Jeremias here recounts at long length, Isaias foretold long before, a hundred and fifty years, which lay between Isaias and Jeremias, saying: “Woe to you, apostate children, saith the Lord, that you would take counsel, and not of me,” etc.
34_interl10660: it is a city of Egypt beyond the Red Sea.
34_interl10661: it is a city in Egypt.
34_interl10663: it shows the mercy of the Lord and the watchfulness and diligence of the prophets.
34_marg2405: A foolish answer: they confess that he speaks in the name of the Lord, nor do they yield, but follow the counsel of their own perversity.
34_marg2406: All heretics, set in the Egypt of this world, that is, in the darkness of error, offer sacrifices not to the true God but to demons, when they write fictions and perverse doctrines to deceive men and subvert the faith. Therefore evils shall come upon them, and they shall be “a desolation, and an astonishment.”
34_interl10664: of the moon, or to Juno, or to Nerecinthia, who is called the wife of Saturn and mother of the gods.
34_interl10665: as if they had received the abundance of good things not from God but from demons.
34_marg2407: The Lord liveth, etc. The prophet, from the word of the Lord, forbids that his name be named by the mouth of the Jews in the land of Egypt; because those who had gone over there against the command of God ought not to have the protection of the Lord in that place. Mystically, moreover, the name of the Lord is not named by the mouth of heretics in the land of Egypt, because neither their speech nor their prayer, while they are in error, is acceptable to God. For “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.” Those therefore who persevere in error shall perish by the sword of strict judgment. But those who, leaving error, return from Egypt into the land of Juda, doing penance and thereafter holding the catholic faith, shall be saved.
34_marg2408: The word which Jeremias spoke, etc. Baruch, still unpractised in bearing the sufferings he was to undergo, was afraid of the calamity of captivity which was hanging over them in the time of Joakim the son of Josias, king of Juda; whence he complains that sorrow has been added to his sorrow; and he is answered by the Lord that he seeks peace for himself to no purpose, when the whole people labours under the sickle of tribulations. He signifies, moreover, those who in the pressure of the tribulations or persecutions with which the Church is burdened in the present waver in faintheartedness, seeking the consolation which is promised in the future; whence: “You shall be made sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”
34_marg2409: Josephus. The king of the Egyptians, when he had returned from the battle, summoned Joachaz to him from a city of Syria called Emath, and suddenly bound him, and gave the kingdom to his elder brother by the same father, named Joakim, and laid upon the province a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one of gold. Joakim paid this money. But Joachaz he led away into Egypt, where he died, having reigned three months and ten days. The mother of Joakim was called Zabum, of the city of Abima. He was by nature unjust and most wicked, neither holy toward God nor gentle toward men. And when he was in the fourth year of his reign, a certain man named Nabuchodonosor received the rule of Babylon; at the same time he came with great equipment to the city of Circha, which is by the Euphrates, to fight against the king of the Egyptians, Nichan, for all Syria was under him. And when the king of Babylon learned the purpose of Nichan, he was not at all afraid, but came with a strong arm to the Euphrates. When the encounter was made, he was defeated and lost many thousands. And the king of Babylon, crossing the Euphrates, took all Syria as far as Pelusium, except Judea. But in the fourth year of Nabuchodonosor, which was the eighth of Joakim, he encamped against the Jews with a great army, to exact tribute from Joakim or else to fight. But Joakim, fearing his threats and desiring peace, gave him the tribute which he had received for three years. But in the third year, hearing that the Egyptians would again fight against Babylon, he did not pay the tribute, but was deceived by the hope of the Egyptian war; for the Egyptians did not presume at all to fight against him.
34_interl10666: as if you will not be endangered there.
34_marg2410: The word which was made, etc. Rabanus. Hitherto the prophet has dealt in mixed fashion, for the sake of the fitness of the narrative, with Juda and Israel, with the Chaldeans and Egyptians. From here he prophesies the word of the Lord against the nations and provinces, that is, to Egypt, the Palestines, the Moabites, the children of Ammon, Idumea, Cedar and Elam, and at last to Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans, that they may know that they have acted against the will of the Lord, and what vengeance they are to suffer. First, then, he turns his speech to Egypt, which was the greatest scandal to the Jews, marking when this utterance was made: namely in the fourth year of Joakim the son of Josias, when Pharao Nechao, king of Egypt, fought at Charchamis with Nabuchodonosor and was overcome.
34_interl10671: against Jerusalem or the land of the Chaldeans.
34_interl10672: as if it boasted that it would cover and destroy Judea and the land of the Chaldeans.
34_interl10675: the proud, who trust in their own power and in the neighbouring provinces, Egypt and Ethiopia
34_marg2411: Heretics and schismatics, sprung from diverse provinces, vainly plan wars against the city of God. For “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” But in the day of the Lord’s vengeance his sword shall devour flesh. Of which it is said: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” And there shall be a victim of the Lord in the land of the north, by the river Euphrates, that is, the flowing of worldly pleasure, when they are delivered into the hands of him who set his throne in the north, that he may cast them into “the pool of fire and brimstone.”
34_marg2412: Go up into Galaad, etc. It is a mountain to which Jacob came on the seventh day, fleeing from Charran; it lies toward the back of Phenicia and Arabia, joined to the hills of Libanus, and extends through the desert as far as beyond the Jordan, where Sehon king of the Amorrhites dwelt. It fell by lot to the children of Ruben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasses.
34_marg2413: The Greeks call it recina. For “reci” is said of whatever flows. It is a tear exhaled by the sweat of trees, as of the cherry and the mastic and the like. The first resin is the terebinth, the most excellent of all; Arabia produces it, Judea, Syria, Cyprus and Africa, and the islands of the Cyclades. The second is the mastic, which is called mirtrix; this is brought from the island of Chios. The third is that of the pine, of which one kind is pictines, another pictine, one liquid, another dry, and they are brought from Colophon; whence the resin took the name colophonia. Resin, moreover, is fit for wounded bodies and is used for medicine; whence: “Is there no balm in Galaad?” Resin, therefore, is put for penance and for the medicine of conversion to God. Hence the prophet exhorts Egypt and the neighbouring provinces to do penance; otherwise they vainly look for medicines from false gods, because they will receive from them not health but confusion.
34_marg2414: The nations have heard, etc. As though the comfort of the idols had failed, she fell before her enemies, and in mutual slaughter the strong fell with the strong. So heretics, who are ever at discord and turn about in various error, tearing one another, receive not the victory of truth, but, captives of error, fall together into the pit of perdition.
34_interl10676: a city given over to magic arts
34_marg2415: As if to say: you who have heard my prophecy, announce to Pharaoh that the time is at hand, and the tumult of war.
34_interl10679: because his people was handed over into the hands of enemies
34_interl10680: as they ought to exhort one another to battle, so they exhort one another to flight
34_interl10681: Nabuchodonosor, who, foolish and without heart, ascribes the victory, which is to be ascribed to God, to his gods
34_marg2416: For as Thabor, etc. That is, from the comparison of fruitful places, as if sunk in the sea, understand the great ruin of the power of the Egyptians.
34_marg2417: Thabor is the boundary of Zabulon, a mountain in the midst of the plain of Galilee, lofty with a wonderful roundness, ten miles distant from Diocesarea toward the eastern region. It was also the border between the tribes of Issachar and Nephthali. Carmel is where Nabal the Carmelite lived, and now there is a village named Carmela at the tenth mile from the town of Hebron, lying toward the eastern region, where there is a Roman garrison. Mystically, however, since Thabor is interpreted “coming light,” or “let light come,” and Carmel “tender” or “soft,” or “knowledge of circumcision,” they signify heretics who are proud in the light of worldly knowledge and wisdom, or Jews, soft or delicate, glorying in the circumcision of the flesh, who live under the true pharao and refuse to serve Christ, sunk in the sea of this world and into perpetual damnation.
34_interl10685: Nabuchodonosor, who turns her to flight from the face of arms
34_marg2418: Because the Egyptian people, brought up in luxury, refused the yoke of discipline in untamed wantonness.
34_marg2419: Her hirelings also, etc. The princes of the Egyptians he calls not shepherds but hirelings, who had no care of the flock but gave themselves to avarice and luxury. Therefore they were turned to flight before their enemies. Mystically, however, we can understand by the hirelings of Egypt the feigned shepherds of the Church, pilgrim in this world, who, seeking earthly gain, do not presume to defend the sheep committed to them against the ravagers; whence: “But the hireling, and he that is not the shepherd, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and flieth.”
34_marg2420: His voice, as of brass, etc. Vengeance has come upon the historical Egypt by the just judgment of God, but it is also to come upon the spiritual Egypt on the day of judgment, which Scripture now proclaims as future, clear in the whole world; whence his voice is fittingly compared to sounding brass, which rings more loudly than the other metals, and the day of judgment will sound more strongly than all the earlier rebukes. For then God “shall come manifestly, and shall not keep silence.”
34_marg2421: “A fire shall burn before him: and a mighty tempest shall be round about him.” Then the angels will hasten to “gather out of his kingdom all scandals,” and the unfruitful trees will be cut down by the axes of a strict examination. Then the useless wood will be cut down, because “every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire.” And the multitude of the lost, who like locusts raise themselves up in a short flight, will be plunged into hell, and then the thought of all carnal men, which rests on the pleasures of the world, will be made plain, and will be handed over to be punished with the devil; whence it follows: The daughter of Egypt is confounded, etc.
34_interl10687: because they have been multiplied beyond number
34_interl10689: Nabuchodonosor and the Chaldeans; for these destroyed everything and overthrew the state of the kingdom
34_marg2422: Although it seems to intimate that the kingdom of the Egyptians was not destroyed beyond repair by Nabuchodonosor, since afterwards there were kings there down to Augustus, yet in a higher sense it designates the Christian times, when the worship of God was restored in the Egypt of this world, to practise which man was born; of which Isaias: “The Lord shall strike Egypt with a scourge, and shall heal it,” etc.
34_marg2423: And thou, fear not, etc. This promise does not fit the Jews well, who are scattered over the whole world and wasted away, and have neither kingdom nor priesthood. But it fits the Christian people, which is gathered from all nations and returns from the captivity of error to the land of the Church, where it shall rest in hope and prosper by the success of virtues, and shall not fear the adversary, trusting in its God. It will not indeed be consumed, but like gold which passes through the fire it will be purified and proved. Yet we can say that that old generation will not be utterly consumed before the day of judgment, because “blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles should come in,” and then all Israel shall be saved.
34_marg2424: The word of the Lord that came to Jeremias the prophet, etc. Jeremias, like Isaias and Ezechiel, foretells the coming plagues to the neighbouring nations, because they harassed the people of God and rejoiced in his adversity. So to the Palestines, as before to the Egyptians, he foretells the coming captivity.
34_interl10691: so that by multitude and violence it overwhelms everything
34_interl10692: with death hanging over each one
34_interl10693: because the noise of the enemy will overcome the voice of those weeping
34_interl10694: that is, it was permitted to no one to take care of another, since the enemy raged against each one singly
34_interl10695: because the Palestines came from Cappadocia
34_interl10696: their wealth and manly strength having been taken away
34_marg2425: He shows that Tyre and Sidon belong to the Palestines, although Tyre fell to the lot of Nephthali, and Sidon, the boundary of the Chanaanites, to the lot of Aser; but he did not possess it, because he was not able to drive out the enemies.
34_marg2426: In which the Cappadocians dwelt, its former inhabitants having been slain; this is the boundary of the Chanaanites near Egypt, and it fell by lot to Juda, but he did not obtain it, because the Enachim, that is, the giants of the Philistines, resisted most strongly; and it is to this day a notable city of Palestine, although it was prophesied of it: Gaza shall be an everlasting mound; yet where it formerly stood hardly any traces remain. For it has been built in another place.
34_interl10698: from the voice of joy and gladness
34_interl10699: a city of Palestine in the lot of Juda, but it did not have it, because it could not overcome its inhabitants
34_marg2427: Baldness is come, etc. It signifies that a plague is coming upon heretics and schismatics and all enemies of the Church, because they have prepared snares for the confessors of Christ, have brought wars, and, the devil kindling them, many kinds of persecutions. 34_marg2429: As there is a carnal and a spiritual circumcision, so there is a carnal and a spiritual Moab. Moab is interpreted “from the father” or “paternal water,” as one conceived of incest and drunkenness, as if the father were absent and unknowing. The king of the Moabites invited the soothsayer Balaam to curse, who prophesied this among other things against Moab: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall rise up out of Israel: and shall strike the chiefs of Moab.” Moab signifies secular wisdom, of which it is said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise”; which, having as its author a sense that is generated from the knowledge of God, seems indeed to be born of the father, but because it is an adulterer and an adversary to the people of God, it is begotten of incest and a cave and night; whence according to Isaias it perished in the night, that is, in everlasting error, as the Egyptians were overwhelmed by the waves “from the morning watch,” that is, by night. And Lot, when Sodom was perishing by night, came to Segor, and the sun rose upon him. Hence Isaias: “Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, Moab is silent.” It is to be noted that Nabo is interpreted “sitting” or “prophecy”; Chariathiarim, “city” or “village of woods”; Hesebon, “thoughts”; Luith, “of the cheeks”; Oronaim, “hole of sorrow.” Since therefore every doctrine contrary to the truth, without the inspiration of God, is born of human sense in the darkness of error, it is laid waste by night, and its arguments, that is, its walls, are destroyed by ecclesiastical discourse, that they may fall silent in everlasting silence, and their making may be turned to penance and tears, over Nabo, that is, prophecy or sitting, namely their teachers, and over Chariathiarim, where there are no fruitful trees but a barren wood; there will be wailing and lamentation, and all the ornaments of eloquence will be taken away, that they may remain naked and deformed. And if they seemed to have any manliness in the beard, it is shaved off, and by the ecclesiastical man it is proved effeminate and weak. They are girded with the sackcloth of penance, and on the housetops and doctrines in which they believed themselves lofty, and in the streets of the spacious way that leads to death, there will be wailing; and they will not go up through pride, but will go down into weeping. Then they will understand all their vain thoughts, which Hesebon means, and the fall and the ascent of pride, so that their voice will be heard even to the evil works they have done and the command which they thought to be God’s, condemning themselves by their own confession. And when they have done penance, which is meant by Luith, that is, the tears of the cheeks, they will come up to the altar, and as from a hole of sorrow at the entrance raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, saying: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.”

34_marg2433: Sloth is born of torpor, fraud of private affection; the lesser love of God heightens the former, and self-love in its own right stirs up the latter. For he commits fraud in the work of God who, loving himself inordinately, hastens by what he does rightly to the goods of a passing reward. But this fraud is committed in three ways, because either the silent favour of the human heart, or the breath of applause, or some external thing is desired. Against which it is said through the prophet: “that shaketh his hands from all bribes”; for fraud is not only in the receiving of money, nor is a gift only one thing. There are three receivings of gifts for which men hasten by fraud. For a gift is favour won from the heart, from thought; a gift from the mouth is glory through applause; a gift from the hand is a reward through giving. But the just man shakes his hands from every gift, because in what he does rightly he seeks to receive neither empty glory from the human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor a giving from the hand. He alone does not commit fraud in the work of God who, while he is watchful in zeal for good action, longs neither for the rewards of a bodily thing, nor for words of praise, nor for human favour. Therefore, since our good deeds themselves cannot escape the sword of lurking guilt unless they are fortified daily by anxious fear, it is rightly said through Job: I feared all my works, as though I had done them rightly in God’s sight, but what I have secretly endured in them I do not know. For often our good deeds perish by the robbery of fraud, because earthly desires thrust themselves into right actions; often they fail when sloth intervenes, and waste away as love grows cold.

34_marg2460: Against Idumea, etc. Tropologically. Idumea is earthly and fleshly delight, which rises up against the spirit, that we may not do the things that are of the spirit; and it hastens to draw to itself the soul set in the midst, rebelling against the sons of Juda, to whom it was formerly subject, and it remembers its ancient grief against those who, departing from the flesh, follow the spirit. Therefore the Lord stretches out his hand over Idumea, to reduce it to desolation, and Theman, which is interpreted failing, and Dedan, that is, kinship, that they may serve the house of Juda. For “Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated.” The Lord loves Jacob because he supplants the fleshly and earthly, and receives its blessing. For first we live according to the flesh, afterwards according to the spirit. For vices come first, then the virtues by which the vices are overwhelmed. For the heart of man is inclined to evil from youth; but mature age condemns the errors of youth; whence: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember.” It is to be known, however, that Jacob received the first blessing, Esau the second, and at the end it is said to him: you shall be your brother’s servant. For when the flesh has been made subject to the spirit, Idumea will pass into Judea, and the flesh will serve reason.

34_marg2471: Damascus is undone, etc. Damascus is interpreted cup of blood or blood of sackcloth; all of which suit the heathens, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty and did works worthy of mourning and sackcloth. In the book of Days the history tells that when the year was completed the army of Syria went up against Joas king of the Jews, and came to Jerusalem and killed all its princes and sent all the spoil to the king of Damascus, though it had come with a few men; and God delivered into their hands a very great multitude, because they had forsaken the Lord God their Father. For after the end of the acceptable year, in which the gospel of Christ was preached, an army of the Gentiles went up from Damascus, with few men, against Juda and Jerusalem, who had forsaken the Lord; and the churchmen took away all their laws and the riches of the prophets and sent them to the king of Damascus; for in comparison with the whole world the faithful were still few, and yet the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands, because they forsook the Son of God, who was foretold through the prophets. Therefore by Damascus is signified the calling of the Gentiles, who, first lovers of blood, after they believed in Christ ceased to be a city of their former way of life; whence Isaias: “and shall be as a ruinous heap of stones.” For as a heap of stones is piled up from scattered stones, so from all nations a heap of believers is gathered in the ruin of the Jews who are falling, while the Gentiles rise.

For it is in Babylon when it is confounded and troubled, and, peace having been forsaken, endures the wars of the passions. To such souls it is said: “Flee ye from the midst of Babylon, and let every one save his own life”; for while it is in Babylon it cannot be saved. But he who there remembers Jerusalem groans and says: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” For it is impossible for one set in Babylon to sing to God with instruments; the instruments of God’s hymns are idle there; whence: “On the willows in the midst thereof we hung up our instruments.” Our instruments are hung up while we are in Babylon, on the willows of its rivers. But if we come to Jerusalem, to the place of vision and peace, we shall play instruments, sing psalms, play the harp, and always praise God. And as the soul of the sinner is in Babylon, so the soul of the just is in Judea; but according to the measure of faith and life, they are separated in Judea itself into places differing among themselves. For one is in Dan, which is in the farthest part of Judea, or in the higher places, somewhat better, or in the middle borders of Judea, or around Jerusalem. But the most blessed of all is he who stands in the midst of Jerusalem. But he who is a sinner and weighed down by exceeding crimes is in Babylon; he who has not yet climbed to the summit of sins is in Egypt and dwells in its parts. And as those who are in Judea do not possess equal places (for one is in Dan, another in Nephthali, another in the borders of Gad), so in Egypt one dwells in Taphnis, another in Memphis, another in Syene, another in Bubastis.

34_marg2490: How is the hammer broken, etc. The hammer of the whole earth is the devil; but there is one who cares nothing for the hammer of the whole earth, namely a man standing upon walls of adamant, and in his hand is adamant. The story relates that adamant is stronger than every striking hammer, unbruised and unconquered, persevering, although the devil the hammer stands over it and the dragon is set upon it, as though it were untameable within; nothing so much does the perfect adamant suffer, standing in the hand of the Lord and in his sight. So there are two things contrary to the just adamant, the hammer and the anvil; whence it is said in the Proverb of those who are pressed by anxieties: they are between the hammer and the anvil. But the just man cares nothing for the hammer and the anvil, whose virtue shines the more the more he is struck. But Moses could not break the hammer of the whole earth, nor Abraham before him, nor Josue after him, nor any of the prophets; but Christ broke it, and the prophet, wondering at this, says: “How is the hammer of the whole earth broken!” First broken, then destroyed. When the devil said, “All these will I give thee, if falling down thou wilt adore me,” etc., he did not destroy it but only broke it, when he departed from him for a time; and afterwards he came, and then he was also destroyed. It is broken by each one of us when we are brought by the Lord into the Church and advance in faith. But it is destroyed and ground small when we come to perfection.

34_marg2493: The same: He hath opened the treasure, etc. In the treasures of the Lord are vessels of wrath; outside the treasure are sinning vessels, which are not vessels of wrath but lesser ones. For they are servants who know not the will of the Lord and do it not. But he who enters the Church is either a vessel of wrath or of mercy; he who is outside is neither of mercy nor of wrath. I therefore seek another name for it: “The Lord of hosts,” it says, “hath a work to be done in the land of the Chaldeans.” According to different understandings, an earthly place is spoken of or named in many ways; and as Christ, by a different reckoning, has many names, though in the underlying subject he is one, yet various in his powers, so, by reason of the malice of the human race, earthly business, though one in the underlying subject, is yet very many by the diversity of understanding. For Christ is one underlying subject, but in one sense a physician, whence: “They that are well have no need of a physician,” etc.; in another a shepherd, because he is over the irrational; in another a king, because he rules the rational; in another the true vine, because men grafted into him bear abundant fruit; and the like. Since, then, in Christ there are very many understandings of different names and the underlying subject is one, so earthly business is one in the underlying subject but, according to understanding, very many. Often, too, in allegorizing, we have said that Babylon is earthly business, which is always confused with vices, afflicting Egypt; and Chaldea, because many consecrate to the stars what is done on earth and assert that it happens by their nod. Everyone, then, who thinks that the stars make men lustful, adulterers, chaste, or the like, is in the land of the Chaldeans. God therefore threatens especially those who are in the land of the Chaldeans; but advancing Abraham to better things, he says: I am he who brings thee out from the land of the Chaldeans. God is able to bring us out of the land of the Chaldeans, and let us believe that no other dispenses our life according to the qualities of merits. The work of the Lord of hosts, then, is in the land of the Chaldeans, because his times are come: open her storehouses, that is, the teachings of nativities; search her as a cave, and destroy her. He who rejects the reckonings of birthdays, who uses the word of truth against them, who shows that what the astrologers owe is false, who teaches that the judgments of God are unsearchable and cannot be comprehended by all, who asserts that the stars are not the cause of what happens upon earth, especially of what befalls Christians, carries out the command of the Lord.

34_marg2500: Flee from the midst of Babylon, etc. After the plagues of Babylon he turns the exhortation to the Jews historically and to the faithful mystically, that they may flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, of worldly confusion.
34_marg2501: Not by degrees, that is, not step by step, but swiftly go out, whoever of you have a soul confused by the passion of various vices; the word is directed to you. It can happen that one is in Babylon, but when he is on the farthest borders he seems in a manner to be outside Babylon. But it is another thing to be in the middle of Babylon, so that the space is equal on every side, and to dwell in its navel, as it were in the middle of the heart of a living creature. As the middle of a living creature is the heart, and Luke calls the heart of the earth the middle of the earth. As it seems to be said in Ezechiel: Tyre set in the heart of the sea; and now sinners ought to flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, from its heart. Flee therefore from the midst of Babylon, that leaving the middle you may begin to be on the borders, not in the middle. For he who is deeply sunk in vices is a dweller in the middle of Babylon; he who little by little leaves evil and turns his nature to better things, and begins not so much to possess virtues as to desire them, flees from the midst of Babylon, yet does not depart. By expounding in this way we must believe that the sacred writings have not even one tittle empty of the wisdom of God. For he who says: “thou shalt not appear empty before me,” much more does he himself speak nothing empty. The prophets, receiving of his fullness, sang what had been taken from the fullness. Therefore the sacred volumes always breathe the spirit of fullness. And there is nothing that does not descend from the fullness of majesty. And they breathe to those who have eyes to see heavenly things, and ears to hear divine things, and nostrils to smell those things which belong to the fullness. First, therefore, one must flee from the midst of Babylon, then each one save his soul. Nor did he say only “save,” but according to another edition, “save again.” Because having once tasted salvation, and falling from it by sin, we came into Babylon. Therefore each one must save his soul again, that he may begin to recover what he lost; whence Peter: “receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls,” etc. But it is in us to flee from Babylon, and in our power, if we will, to raise up again what has fallen.
34_marg2502: Origen. Another edition: “be not cast away in her iniquities,” etc. He who is in the injustice of Babylon and has not done penance, it follows that he be cast out; whence it is said elsewhere: “I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God,” not cast out. Here, however, he did not put “be not made abject” but “be not cast out.” For to be cast out is one thing, to be made abject another. What is despised is made abject; what is utterly alien to salvation is cast out. Whence: The leaders of my people shall be cast out of the house of their delights, because of their wicked wills. Their portions shall not profit them, because it is the time of his revenge from the Lord. In a wonderful sense he says that punishments are inflicted for the vengeance of him who suffers them. For when one is not avenged, he is left unpunished; whence: “I will not visit upon your daughters when they shall commit fornication.” God therefore does not punish sinners in anger, but it is expedient so to speak. It is a great anger of God not to endure torments. For he who is punished is punished for this, that he may be amended, even if he is corrected by that which is called the wrath of God. Punishment is promised also to the sinning sons of Christ, lest pardon be denied: “If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments,” etc. See therefore how he is not yet worthy of punishment who still commits criminal wickedness and does not pay for it. For the visitation of God is shown by the usual torments. But as for him who sins and is corrected, I do not know what of punishment may run to him.
34_marg2503: The same, etc. God himself does not repay all; there are those to whom he repays through others, either punishing or healing by sorrow; whence: “he sent upon them the fury of his wrath.” Fury and wrath, distress, a sending in through the worst angels; to others perhaps he repays through good angels, as to those who are punished for their crimes. There are times when, the service of ministers set aside, he himself repays, as now to Babylon. When the wounds are slight and the cure ready, the physician sends a servant, sends a disciple, and heals by him. Sometimes he who is healed needs cutting and the knife; yet he does not come himself, but uses as minister one of the disciples who is able to cure. But when the wounds are incurable and there is deep rot in the dead flesh, when he needs neither servants nor disciples but the hands of the master himself, then he himself, with his loins girded, is roused to cut the wound with his hands. Likewise when the sins are lesser, God uses ministers; but when they are graver, then he himself hastens to the repayment.

34_marg2504: Babylon a golden cup, etc. Babylon is not always a golden cup, nor always in the hand of the Lord. For when she has come to vengeance and been placed in the hand of the Lord, she will be made the earth which is touched upon in Job. Nor is she continually held in the hand of the Lord, but only then when the Lord shall restore to her what she deserves.
34_marg2505: A golden cup of Babylon, etc. Nabuchodonosor, wishing to deceive men by the cup of Babylon, did not mix it in a vessel of clay, of iron, of bronze, of tin, or of silver, which surpasses these. He tempered the draught in a golden vessel, so that seeing the beauty of the shining gold you might cling with all your eyes to its appearance, and not consider what it holds within, but seize it and drink unknowing. Understand by the cup of Nabuchodonosor the pestilent words of wicked doctrines: what composition of speech they have, what beauty of eloquence, and you will know how each poet tempered a golden cup and cast in the poison of idolatry and foul speaking, and of those doctrines which kill the soul, and of knowledge falsely so called. But Jesus did the contrary. For knowing the golden cup of the devil, lest anyone coming to the faith should think that the cup of Christ also was such as he had left, and for the likeness of the material should fear error, he took care that this treasure should be held in earthen vessels. Often I have seen a golden cup in the fair adornment of speech, and considering the poisons of its doctrines, I have detected the cup of Babylon.
34_marg2506: Making all the earth drunk, etc. See all men drunk: we are made drunk by anger and sadness, we are made drunk and go out of our mind by love, concupiscence, vainglory. Observe that all the earth is full of sins, and you will not ask how Babylon made all the earth drunk. For the just man is not in the earth but above the earth, having his conversation in heaven; nor will it be fitting to say to him, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go”, but, You are heaven and into heaven you shall go; for he bears the image of the heavenly. The golden cup therefore makes all the earth drunk, that is, we are all made drunk by it as long as we are earth.
34_marg2507: The same, etc. As in those who drink bodily wine beyond measure we see the motion of the drunken body, the feet staggering, the head and temples heavy, the mouth loose, and the words broken off with clinging lips, so those who have drunk of the golden cup of Babylon are unsteady in step, weakened in mind, with wavering effort; they hold nothing firm, but are always driven about in confusion, uncertain. The nations have drunk, and therefore they have staggered.

This is what he says: take balm for her correction, if so she may be healed. Where are the heretics, who introducing certain natures assert that there is a matter past hope which does not receive salvation at all? But God does not despise Babylon; for he commands the physicians to take balm, if so she may be healed. Some of them therefore, taking the balm of Babylon’s correction, did what had been unprepared, hearing that she could receive health; but because she would not be cured, the good physicians make their excuse and say: We have cured Babylon, and she is not healed.

34_marg2509: We have cured Babylon, etc. See lest at some time God command the angels to prepare medicines for your languishing soul, if so it may be healed, and they answer him: We have cured Babylon, showing that your soul is confounded by passion and is not healed. They do not blame the knowledge of the art nor the power of the balm, but you, who would not obey them. The angels of God are physicians under the great Physician, willing to cure our souls of their vices; these we ourselves drive away when we do not acquiesce in their counsels; seeing that they are losing their labour, they say to one another: Let us forsake her, etc., as if to say: a medicine was handed to us by God that we might cure the human soul; we have applied helps and medicines; she is stubborn, she will not observe what we say; our zeal is not followed by effect; let us go every man to his own land, that is, to his own domestic and nearer business. Beware when a physician or an angel of God, or he to whom the care of the word is entrusted for the medicines of salvation, forsakes you; for if they forsake you and say, Let us go every man to his own land, because “her judgment hath reached even to the heavens,” it is plain that the departure of the physician is your condemnation, beyond remedy, since you are unwilling to be cured. So it will befall you as it befalls those who are despaired of by physicians, and, indulging the pleasure of the disease, are plunged into worse. Often a prudent physician comes to the sick man and, as far as the art allows, does not cease his diligence of medicine; but if the sickness is so great that it resists the cure, or the sick man through impatience of pain does the contrary of what is ordered, the physician despairing leaves him, lest he expire under his hands and he seem guilty of his death. Let us not therefore die in the hands of the holy angels, lest they forsake us in despair and say: there is no plaster to apply, neither oil nor bandage, because her judgment has reached to heaven, is lifted up even to the stars. He who has a small sin does not carry his judgment up to heaven and the stars, for it is small and lowly. But he who grows in wickedness grows also in judgment, and together with the vices the punishment is increased. And because he sins so much that his judgment is lifted up to heaven, and through his impiety, resisting God, he ascends to the heights, God brings forth his judgment to humble what has been exalted.

34_marg2522: Therefore behold the days come, etc. He enumerates the plagues that are to come upon Babylon, and upon her nobles, her leaders and magistrates, and all the people, because, slain by various punishments, they will sleep the sleep of eternal death. Mystically he here announces the ruin of the faithless city, which the devil built from the beginning, and through which he has diligently fought against the city of God, because, when the elect of God are delivered, the wicked city will be plunged into eternal punishment; whence John in the Apocalypse: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen,” etc.; and after a few words: “Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins, and that you receive not of her plagues,” etc.

34_marg2523: Thus shall Babylon sink, etc. Historically, Babylon was not sunk in the Euphrates, although it was reduced to a wilderness; but he foretells the eternal destruction of the spiritual Babylon, which will be plunged into the depth of hell with its prince the devil; whence John in the Apocalypse: “A mighty angel took up a stone, as it were a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying: With such violence as this shall Babylon be thrown down.”
34_marg2524: The history which relates that Sedechias was taken and Jerusalem laid waste by the Chaldeans is fully contained in the Book of Kings.
34_marg2525: And it came to pass in the ninth year, etc. The number nine, less than ten, signifies the imperfection of the law, as eleven signifies transgression. Rightly, then, Nabuchodonosor besieged the city in the ninth year of the reign of Sedecias, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, because when evil pastors know the decalogue and neglect to fulfil it, it must be that the ancient enemy, with his army, surrounds the people committed to them, hemming them in with a fortification of errors and vices. And the famine of the word of God prevails in the city, when the bread of doctrine is not freely dispensed, and the city is broken into, and the men of war flee by night. For when the temptation of the devil has broken through, the guardians of the peoples, who ought to have defended the city with the sword of the word of God, hemmed in by the darkness of ignorance and of sins, flee by night; and seeing the wolf coming, they leave the sheep.
34_marg2526: By the way of the gate, etc. He secretly rebukes the sloth of teachers who, placed between the walls of the two testaments, seek not to wage war but to flee, and to abound in delights (which the garden signifies) rather than to leave off ease for the shield of faith.
34_marg2527: And the army pursued, etc. In the Book of Kings it is read thus: Sedecias fled by the way that leads to the plains of the wilderness, and the army of the Chaldeans pursued, and overtook him in the plain of Jericho; and all the warriors that were with him were scattered, etc. When malignant spirits surround the people, the ruler does not flee to the mountains, of which it is said: “Mountains are round about it, so the Lord is round about his people,” but to the plains of the wilderness, that is, to the broad and spacious way that leads to death. And “he is overtaken in the plain of Jericho, and all the men of war that were with him were scattered, and left him”: when the virtues desert the man whom they ought to have defended, he is taken in the wilderness, and in the plain of Jericho, that is, in wantonness, or in the failing of carnal desire and way of life. For Jericho is interpreted “moon,” and signifies the failing of the flesh. Whence he who went down from Jerusalem into Jericho is described as having fallen among robbers. “So they took the king and carried him to the king of Babylon to Reblatha,” etc.

34_marg2529: And in the fifth month, etc. The order of time agrees with the reason of the vengeance: in the fifth month the city is laid waste which despised the Pentateuch; on the tenth day of the month, because it did things contrary to the decalogue of the law, flattering itself with security because of the dwelling of the holy places; whence above: “Trust not in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.”
34_marg2530: When scripture tells the captivity of Sedecias, it announces the order of the inward captivity. For the king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of inmost confusion, who first slays the sons before the eyes of the one looking on, because he often so kills good works that the mind itself, which is taken captive, sees with grief that it is losing them. For while the mind often groans, yet, overcome by the delights of its flesh, it loses the good things it loves and has begotten, and considers the losses it suffers, yet does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon, but is struck down while it sees the perpetration of wickedness. By the practice of sin it is at times brought to this, that it is deprived even of the light of reason itself; whence the king of Babylon, the sons of Sedecias having first been slain, puts out his eyes, because the malignant spirit, having first taken away good works, takes away also the light of understanding; which Sedecias rightly suffers in Reblatha, which is interpreted “this much.” For at times even the light of all reason is shut out, because the man is weighed down by evil habit and by the multitude of his iniquity.
34_marg2531: Nabuzardan the general came, etc. By the just judgment of God, Nabuzardan, the general of the armies of the king of Babylon, came upon Jerusalem and burnt the house of the Lord, when the ancient enemy, the king of confusion, the prince of all the wicked, invades the flock of the faithful; and the king’s house and the houses of Jerusalem, that is, the rulers and those who seemed to dwell in the vision of peace, inflamed with covetousness, he overthrows; “every house he burnt with fire,” that is, the conscience of each with the flame of unlawful love.

34_marg2534: Rabanus. In that he describes the making of the pillars with the capitals and the network and the pomegranates, he shows it to be a mystical work; for as the pillars signify teachers, so the capitals, that is, their uppermost part, are the hearts of faithful teachers, and the network expresses the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit, as the pomegranates the sweetness of the virtues. All these the ancient enemy strives through his ministers to take away from the temple of God. But if anyone wishes to know this more fully, let him read our work on the Book of Kings, where what the holy fathers thought of these things is set out.

34_marg2540: And the king of Babylon struck them, etc. The king of Babylon aims, by leading away those whom he tears from the Church, to bring them to the killing of perpetual death.
34_marg2541: This is the people, etc. Rabanus. Nabuchodonosor laid Judea waste three times. First, when he led Joachim, who is also Heliachim, the son of Josias, bound in chains to Babylon, with the vessels of the Lord, which he placed in his temple. Second, when he carried Joachim, surnamed Jechonias, his son, to Babylon with his mother and the princes and the eunuchs, and the most precious vessels of the house of the Lord. Third, when he took Sedecias and blinded him, killed his sons, and burnt the house of the Lord and destroyed Jerusalem; whence Jeremias says that at the first there were carried away three thousand and thirty-two, at the second eight hundred and thirty-two, at the third seven hundred and forty-five. And reckoning the sum he says that there were four thousand six hundred souls. What was done historically he hints at spiritually: because all who by error defile the faith of the Holy Trinity, and do not keep the teaching of the gospels, and despise the perfection of good works, deservedly serve the king of confusion, who leads those deprived of the light of knowledge into the captivity of everlasting confusion, and thrusts them back into the prison of hell, where the damned groan forever.

34_marg2542: And it came to pass, etc. It signifies the wonderful power of God, which exercises its just judgments through good and wicked alike. For as he condemned Sedecias, incorrigible and disobedient to the prophets, through Nabuchodonosor to blindness and perpetual captivity, so through Evilmerodach he mercifully looked upon Joachim, who, although he had been a sinner, yet, taking thought for the people and the city, gave himself and his mother over to the king of Babylon, and, now corrected, freeing him from his punishments restored him to rest and honor.
